Professor, Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability
Associate Director, Data Institute for Societal Challenges




Ph.D., Forest Ecology, Oregon State University
M.S., Quantitative Resource Management, University of Washington
B.A., Environmental Science, University of Virginia




Dr. Mike Wimberly is a Professor in the Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability at the University of Oklahoma and the head of the EcoGRAPH research group. His research combines ecological models with satellite Earth observations to address scientific questions and develop applications in the fields of public health and natural resource management. Areas of study include wildfire and vegetation dynamics in temperate and tropical forest ecosystems, drivers and consequences of urbanization and agricultural expansion, and the effects of land use and climate on vector-borne disease transmission. Dr. Wimberly builds upon this research to create software that applies geospatial data and analytics for decision support. He has developed disease early warning systems to predict West Nile virus outbreaks in the United States and malaria in Ethiopia, used Earth observations to monitor forest degradation and urban growth in West Africa, and designed spatial simulation models to project future landscapes under scenarios of global change.

title: EPIDEMIA
text:
Outbreaks of malaria are often linked to climate variations and land use changes that affect the life cycles of the mosquito vector and the Plasmodium parasite. Early warning of the timing and locations of these epidemics can facilitate more effective targeting of resources for disease prevention, control, and treatment. We have developed the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Monitoring for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system to support malaria forecasting in epidemic-prone regions of Ethiopia. EPIDEMIA uses machine-learning techniques with malaria surveillance data and environmental data from Earth-observing satellites to determine the relationships between climate variations and malaria outbreaks. The system provides an open-source software toolbox for data harmonization, predictive analytics, and report generation implemented in the R language and software environment. Remotely sensed data are accessed through a Google Earth Engine application that supports cloud-based data processing and produces downloadable summaries for use with EPIDEMIA. The software is usable with existing public health surveillance databases and can be run on a variety of computer systems.
 Examples of remotely-sensed environment data used in EPIDEMIA, including MODIS land surface temperature (left), and rainfall data from the Global Precipitation Mission (Right).
The first step in implementing EPIDEMIA is to acquire historical epidemiological and environmental data for the region of interest and develop a harmonized dataset for modeling. These data are then used to identify geographic strata for modeling and calibrate the predictive models. To generate weekly forecasts, the system is updated with recent data, model predictions are generated for the upcoming twelve weeks, and the results are used to generate a formatted report with maps and charts. Forecasting is fully automated, and the necessary data processing, modeling, and report generation steps are carried out by running a single script. A separate validation module can be used to generate retrospective forecasts and evaluate their predictive skill using historical data.
 Flowchart of the EPIDEMIA system illustrating the steps for generating a weekly forecast.
EPIDEMIA 1.0 was developed by an interdisciplinary team that includes scientists from the University of Oklahoma, along with collaborators from Ethiopian public health agencies, non-governmental organizations, and universities. The system was piloted and tested through a demonstration project in the Amhara region of Ethiopia. We worked with the United States Agency for International Development and the U.S. President’s Malaria Initiative to develop a roadmap for scaling up malaria early warning with EPIDEMIA to a national level. This work evaluated national-level malaria surveillance datasets, and engaged with a variety of stakeholders in Ethiopia. This page provides links to project outputs, including software code, documentation, and data.
We are currently working on a NASA-supported project to develop an updated version of the software that will provide substantial upgrades. The main objectives of this work are to improve the user interface to streamline modeling and provide interactive visualization for decision support, integrate new sources of environmental data from satellite Earth observations, incorporate novel predictive AI approaches for outbreak detection and forecasting, and expand the scope to include additional climate sensitive diseases besides malaria. For more information visit the EPIDEMIA 2.0 page.

title: ArboMAP
text:
West Nile virus (WNV) is endemic in the United States and poses a persistent threat to public health. In particular, the Northern Great Plains are a hot spot for WNV transmission, and South Dakota has the highest long-term incidence of West Nile neuroinvasive disease in the country. We have conducted research on WNV epidemiology to explore the environmental risk factors that affect transmission to humans. The spatial and temporal distributions of vector mosquitoes and bird hosts, and the risk of disease in humans, are strongly influenced by temperature, humidity, vegetation, soils, and land use. These relationships can be quantified using mathematical models and applied to develop maps of WNV risk and forecast the probability of future outbreaks.
 Conceptual diagram of information flow through the ArboMAP system.
We have applied these results to develop a WNV early warning system for South Dakota that combines environmental monitoring with mosquito surveillance to produce weekly maps of WNV risk during the transmission season. The Arbovirus Mapping and Prediction (ArboMAP) system ingests gridded meteorological data using Google Earth Engine, a cloud-based platform for Earth science data analysis. Mosquito abundance and testing data are uploaded from locations throughout the state via a web-based surveillance platform. Statistical models are used to estimate the mosquito infection rate from recent surveillance data, and to predict the number of human cases based on mosquito infection rate, temperature, and humidity. These models are implemented using the R programming language and software environment, and all code is publicly available via GitHub. This work is supported in part by a grant from the NASA Applied Sciences Public Health and Air Quality Program (NNX15AF74G).
 Prospective WNV forecasts. Black line/Gray shading: prediction with 95% intervals; Red line: Observed cases in 2016 or 2017; Dashed line: Observed cases in 2012; Dotted line: Observed cases in 2015.

title: CHANGE
text:
Climate change has myriad effects on ecosystems worldwide, with natural and human-caused disturbances serving as major drivers. In addition, increasing human exploitation of fire-prone ecosystems is altering fire regimes, increasing human vulnerability, and limiting management options. To better understand the implications of these changes, there is a need for simulation models that can project future landscape dynamics in the context of changing climates and expanding human populations. We developed an integrated land change simulator by coupling a model of natural disturbances and vegetation dynamics (LADS, the LAndscape Dynamics Simulator developed by Mike Wimberly) with a model of human driven land use and land cover change (FORE-SCE, the FOREcasting SCEnarios of future land cover model developed by Terry Sohl at the USGS Center for Earth Resources Observation and Science). The result is a novel model for Simulating Coupled Human and Natural Environments (CHANGE).
 Conceptual diagram of the CHANGE simulation model.
The CHANGE model simulates gridded landscapes classified into discrete land use and land cover (LULC) classes such as developed land, forest, shrubland, and cropland. Transitions between these LULC classes are modeled using a demand-allocation algorithm that was adapted from FOR-SCE. Naturally-vegetated LCLU classes are further divided into vegetation states that represent unique combinations of vegetation structure and species composition. Within these naturally-vegetated areas, succession is modeled deterministically using a state-and-transition model, and wildfires are modeled using a stochastic cellular fire spread algorithm derived from LADS. CHANGE also includes new components for explicitly modeling the human-natural interface (HNI) as a hybrid LULC class. Examples of the HNI include low-density housing in fire-prone forests in the western United States and small-scale agricultural encroachment into tropical forests in West Africa.
 *Output of the CHANGE model with examples of landscape change in the Colorado Front Range: A) Wildland-urban interface expansion, B) Wildfire in the Wildland-urban interface, C) Urban growth, and D) Wildfire outside of the wildland-urban interface.
Note: CHANGE is no longer under active development. Historical code, executables, and parameter files for example scenarios are archived on GitHub.

title: Landscape Epidemiology
text:
Land cover and land use influence infectious disease transmission by shaping the habitats of disease vectors and reservoir hosts and affecting human exposure to pathogens. Vegetation, hydrology, and built environments determine habitat suitability, while human activities such as urbanization, agriculture, and resource extraction modify natural habitats and create new opportunities for disease transmission. Land cover also influences local microclimates, potentially allowing vectors and hosts to persist in regions where broader climatic conditions would otherwise be unsuitable.
 Map of the relative risk of West Nile virus in South Dakota derived from a machine learning model that predicts georeferenced cases using remotely sensed environmental indices (Hess et al. 2018).
Our research has demonstrated how landscape characteristics influence the spatial distribution of mosquito-borne diseases across diverse geographic settings. In the northern Great Plains of the United States, we found that West Nile virus (WNV) incidence was highest in rural valleys dominated by grasslands and lowest in urban and forested mountainous regions (Chuang et al., 2012; Hess et al., 2018). In the Amhara region of Ethiopia, malaria incidence was highest in districts with extensive wetland cover (Midekisa et al. 2014). However, a more localized analysis of malaria transmission in four Ethiopian districts revealed different patterns, with higher incidence in areas characterized by sparse vegetation and particular patterns of human settlement (McMahon et al. 2021). Together, these studies demonstrate that landscape characteristics are important predictors of mosquito-borne disease risk, but their effects depend on geographic context and spatial scale. These findings also highlight the value of satellite Earth observations for identifying environmental risk factors and developing geographically tailored disease risk maps.

title: Urban Expansion Dynamics
text:
Urbanization is transforming landscapes across the Global South, particularly in Africa, where rapidly growing populations are driving widespread expansion of developed land. Although research has traditionally focused on large metropolitan areas, smaller secondary cities are increasingly important centers of urban growth. Our research uses satellite Earth observations to map urban expansion, investigate its underlying drivers, and assess its environmental consequences. We are also developing spatially explicit urban growth models to project future patterns of expansion and evaluate how urbanization and climate change may interact to influence human exposure to heat and infectious diseases (Korah et al. 2024).
 Patterns of infill and sprawl urban expansion for three cities in West Africa (Korah et al. 2024a).
Our research has demonstrated that secondary cities play an increasingly important role in urban expansion and environmental change across West Africa. We developed satellite-based mapping approaches that improve the detection of urban growth in smaller cities compared with existing global land cover products (Korah and Wimberly, 2024b). Analysis of two decades of urban expansion revealed that secondary cities are growing faster and exhibiting more sprawling development patterns than larger primary cities, accounting for an increasing share of developed land (Korah and Wimberly, 2024a). Complementary research in Ghana identified lower land and housing costs and more flexible land allocation as important factors contributing to the growth of secondary cities (Korah et al. 2025). We also demonstrated that urban expansion is a major driver of tree cover loss in Ghana and Nigeria, highlighting the environmental consequences of rapid urban growth (Korah and Wimberly 2026). Together, these findings underscore the importance of including secondary cities in urban planning, environmental monitoring, and projections of future land cover change.

title: Wildfire and Tropical Forest Degradation
text:
Tropical forests in West Africa are increasingly threatened by agricultural expansion, logging, and wildfires, with climate change amplifying their vulnerability to disturbance. These forests experience some of the highest temperatures and longest dry seasons among tropical forest ecosystems, making them particularly susceptible to drought and fire. Our research has documented changing fire regimes and forest degradation across tropical Africa, developed satellite-based approaches for monitoring and predicting forest disturbances, and assessed the long-term consequences of degradation for forest recovery and carbon storage.
 Fire prevention sign located near Pamu-Berekum forest reserve in the Brong-Ahafo region of Ghana.
We fount that fire activity is increasing in tropical African forests, even as it has declined in surrounding savanna ecosystems. In West Africa, vegetation characteristics largely determine the spatial distribution of fires, while climate influences their seasonality and intensity (Dwomoh and Wimberly 2017b). Across the moist African tropics, increasing fire activity has been associated with rising temperatures, atmospheric moisture deficits, and deforestation (Wimberly et al. 2024). Studies in Ghana’s forest reserves have also revealed important feedbacks between fire and forest degradation: disturbances reduce canopy cover and promote the establishment of more flammable vegetation, increasing susceptibility to subsequent fires and potentially driving persistent forest loss (Dwomoh and Wimberly 2017a, Dwomoh et al. 2019). These findings suggest that climate change and human disturbances may reinforce one another, increasing the risk of transitions from closed-canopy forest to more open, fire-prone vegetation.
 Spatial patterns and time series trends of active fire detections from 2003-2021 across the African moist tropics (Wimberly et al. 2024).
We have also advanced satellite-based methods for tracking forest degradation and identifying areas vulnerable to future disturbance. Across the Upper Guinean region of West Africa, we documented widespread declines in woody vegetation and increases in herbaceous cover (Liu et al. 2017). Using Landsat time series, we reconstructed forest disturbance histories across Ghana’s forest reserves, revealing a sharp increase in degradation and forest loss associated with drought and fires in 2016 (Wimberly et al. 2022). Subsequent modeling demonstrated that landscape fragmentation, human population pressure, and drought can be used to identify areas at elevated risk of future disturbance (Wanyama et al. 2023). We also found that biomass recovery following degradation is slow, highlighting the potential for disturbances to produce persistent reductions in forest carbon storage (Wanyama et al. 2025). Together, these studies provide a foundation for anticipating forest degradation and identifying landscapes where conservation and restoration efforts may be most needed.

title: Climate Epidemiology
text:
Climate is an important driver of infectious disease transmission, influencing the geographic distributions of pathogens and their hosts, the seasonal timing of transmission, and the occurrence of disease outbreaks. Understanding this variability is essential for anticipating how infectious diseases respond to short-term weather events, seasonal climate fluctuations, and long-term climate change. Our research has advanced understanding of the climatic drivers of West Nile virus (WNV) in the United States and malaria in Ethiopia and India. Studies of WNV outbreaks in the northern Great Plains demonstrated that disease incidence was highest in areas with warmer temperatures and intermediate precipitation (Wimberly et al. 2008), while subsequent research identified elevated temperatures during both winter and the transmission season as important predictors of outbreaks (Wimberly et al. 2014). Time-series modeling in South Dakota and Louisiana further demonstrated the importance of temperature, precipitation, atmospheric humidity, and wind speed in explaining seasonal and interannual variation in WNV transmission (Davis et al. 2018, Bump et al. 2025).
 Data from the Ahmara Region of Ethiopia illustrating seasonal patterns of temperature and precipitation and their associations with malaria cases (Midekisa et al. 2015).
An important contribution of this work has been demonstrating that the climatic drivers of disease transmission vary across geographic and environmental settings. For example, our research in Ethiopia showed that temperature was a stronger predictor of malaria outbreaks in wetter districts, whereas rainfall and moisture conditions were more influential in drier districts (Midekisa et al. 2015). In the United States, temperature and humidity had positive effects on WNV occurence in a cooler and drier climate versus negative effects in a warmer and more humid climate Bump et al. 2025). These findings highlight the importance of accounting for local environmental conditions rather than assuming that climate–disease relationships are uniform across regions. This research has established a foundation for climate-informed disease forecasting and early warning systems. By integrating environmental observations with disease surveillance data, we have developed predictive models that account for delayed responses to weather conditions and spatial variation in climatic drivers (Midekisa et al. 2012; Davis et al. 2019). These approaches provide a scientific basis for anticipating disease outbreaks and supporting more proactive public health surveillance and response. For more information see the sections on Malaria Early Warning and West Nile Virus Forecasting.

title: Malaria Early Warning
text:
Malaria remains a major public health challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. Strengthening malaria surveillance requires moving beyond reactive responses toward predictive approaches that provide advance warning of outbreaks and support more proactive disease control. Our research has advanced methods for malaria forecasting and outbreak detection by integrating routine disease surveillance with satellite Earth observations and predictive models. Working in the epidemic-prone Amhara region of Ethiopia, we developed and evaluated forecasting approaches that account for geographic variation in the delayed effects of climate on malaria transmission (Midekisa et al. 2012, Davis et al. 2019, Nekorchuk et al. 2021). We also evaluated alternative sources of environmental data (Alemu and Wimberly 2020) and developed informatics tools to make satellite observations more accessible for disease surveillance and forecasting (Liu et al. 2015, Wimberly et al. 2022).
 Time series visualizations for weekly forecasts from the EPIDEMIA system (Merkord et al. 2017).
A major outcome of this research has been the development of the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Monitoring for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system, an open-source platform that translates advances in environmental monitoring and predictive modeling into practical tools for malaria early warning (Merkord et al. 2017). Co-developed with Ethiopian public health partners, EPIDEMIA integrates epidemiological and environmental data to detect emerging outbreaks and generate malaria forecasts up to 12 weeks in advance. Following a pilot implementation in the Amhara region, we worked with national stakeholders to develop a roadmap for scaling malaria early warning across Ethiopia (Wimberly and Nekorchuk 2021). We are now developing EPIDEMIA 2.0, a next-generation platform with improved visualization, modeling capabilities, and interoperability with existing public health information systems. These efforts aim to make malaria forecasting more accessible and actionable, helping public health agencies anticipate outbreaks and better target surveillance and control activities.

title: Mosquito Ecology
text:
Mosquito abundance, behavior, and disease transmission potential are strongly influenced by environmental conditions. Aquatic habitats are essential for larval development, while temperature and atmospheric moisture regulate mosquito physiology, survival, and reproduction (Brown et al. 2023, Huxley et al. 2026). These relationships vary among species and environmental settings, making it essential to understand how local weather, hydrology, and landscape characteristics interact to influence mosquito populations.
Our research has demonstrated substantial differences in the environmental drivers of mosquito abundance across species and geographic regions. In South Dakota, the floodwater mosquito Aedes vexans is strongly associated with wetland habitats and responds to heavy rainfall, whereas Culex tarsalis, an important West Nile virus vector, is associated with grasslands and responds more strongly to temperature (Chuang et al. 2011; Chuang et al. 2012). In Oklahoma, Culex quinquefasciatus is most abundant in highly developed landscapes, while Aedes albopictus is associated with areas of low tree cover; both species are more abundant following periods of warm, humid weather with little rainfall (McMahon et al. 2022). In Georgia, we demonstrated how land cover influences local microclimates, creating fine-scale variation in Aedes albopictus abundance and potential disease transmission (Wimberly et al. 2020).
 Effects of environmental variables from local microclimate, satellite remote sensing, and weather station data on Aedes albopictus and Culex quinquefasciatus abundance. Variables include spectral indices (Indices), land cover (LC), precipitation (Precip), relative humidity (RH), and temperature(T) (McMahon et al. 2022).
An important contribution of this research has been identifying environmental indicators that are more closely linked to mosquito ecology than conventional weather measurements. Variables such as soil moisture, drought indices, and solar radiation can provide stronger predictors of mosquito abundance than temperature and precipitation alone (Bump and Wimberly, 2026). Satellite Earth observations of surface water, vegetation, and land surface temperature can also perform as well as or better than ground-based meteorological measurements (Chuang et al. 2012; McMahon et al. 2022). These findings highlight the importance of selecting ecologically relevant environmental predictors and measuring them at spatial and temporal scales appropriate for understanding mosquito populations and improving abundance forecasts.

title: Urban Health
text:
Urban areas are among the fastest-growing landscapes on the planet, and the transmission of diseases by urban-adapted mosquitoes has increased markedly over recent decades. Our research investigates how urban landscapes influence mosquito habitats, local microclimates, and disease transmission, with an emphasis on understanding the combined effects of environmental and socioeconomic conditions. We integrate satellite Earth observations, ground-based measurements, and disease transmission models to map urban transmission hotspots and anticipate how disease risk may change with urbanization and climate change. In the southeastern United States, we combined satellite observations and in situ microclimate measurements to generate high-resolution temperature maps, which were linked with mechanistic models to characterize neighborhood-level variation in potential dengue transmission (Wimberly et al. 2020).
 Maps of temperature-dependent vectorial capacity (VC(T)) for Athens-Clarke County, GA during four monthly periods in 2018 (Wimberly et al. 2020).
Building on this work, we are collaborating with Courtney Murdock (Cornell University) and Mercedes Pascual (University of Chicago) to investigate urban malaria transmission by Anopheles stephensi in Ahmedabad and Surat, India. This research extends temperature-dependent transmission models to account for the effects of humidity on mosquito water balance and survival. We established a network of indoor and outdoor microclimate sensors in residential neighborhoods to characterize fine-scale temperature and humidity patterns and their relationships with urban land cover (Jamal et al. 2025). Complementary household surveys examine how socioeconomic conditions and domestic water management practices influence malaria risk (Batheja et al. 2026). We are integrating these environmental and socioeconomic data into spatial models to identify urban malaria hotspots and assess how transmission risk varies across neighborhoods. Related research with collaborators in Ethiopia has examined malaria trends in urbanizing environments and the implications of Anopheles stephensi invasion for urban malaria control (Teka et al. 2023).

title: Pyrogeography of the Western United States
text:
Wildfire regimes in western North America are changing in response to climate warming, vegetation shifts, and human alterations of forest landscapes. Our research has investigated the interacting effects of climate, vegetation, and land management on wildfire occurrence and behavior, using satellite remote sensing, spatial analysis, and landscape simulation models. These studies have contributed to understanding how wildfire regimes are changing, how forest management can mitigate fire risk, and how contemporary landscapes compare with historical conditions.
Our research demonstrated that climate change influences wildfire through both direct effects on fire weather and indirect effects on vegetation and fuels. Landscape simulations projected increases in burned area across the western United States, with climate-driven changes in vegetation potentially as important as changes in temperature and fuel moisture (Liu and Wimberly 2015, Liu and Wimberly 2016). In the Colorado Front Range, we also found that climate change and expansion of the wildland–urban interface interact nonlinearly, with warming amplifying the fire risks associated with residential development in fire-prone landscapes (Liu et al. 2015). These findings highlight the importance of considering climate, vegetation dynamics, and human development together when assessing future wildfire risk.
 Projected future fire regimes under climate change for a scenario allowing shifts in vegetation type (left) and a scenario maintaining current vegetation types (right) (Liu and Wimberly 2016).
We also evaluated how forest management influences wildfire behavior and severity. Using satellite observations and fire behavior models, we demonstrated that fuel treatments combining canopy thinning with prescribed burning or mastication were more effective at reducing fire size and severity than treatments addressing canopy or surface fuels alone (Wimberly et al. 2009, Cochrane et al. 2012). Research in eastern Washington revealed contrasting effects of forest roads: although ignitions were more frequent near roads, fire spread and severity were often reduced in their vicinity (Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2012, Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2011, Narayanaraj and Wimberly, 2013). These studies provide insights into how landscape configuration and management practices influence fire risk.
 Maps burn severity derived from satellite remote sensing and fuel treatments for four wildfires in the western United States (Wimberly et al. 2009).
An important contribution of our earlier research was reconstructing historical fire regimes and old-growth forest dynamics in the Pacific Northwest. We developed the Landscape Dynamics Simulator (LADS) to investigate how wildfire shaped forest age structure before widespread logging and fire suppression (Wimberly et al. 2000, Wimberly 2002). Despite the occurrence of large wildfires, simulations indicated that old-growth forests historically occupied approximately 29–52% of forested landscapes, substantially more than their contemporary extent (Wimberly et al. 2004). Subsequent improvements to LADS incorporated mixed-severity fire regimes and explored how climate change could shift forest landscapes beyond their historical range of variability (Wimberly and Kennedy 2008, Kennedy and Wimberly 2009, Wimberly and Liu 2014). This work established a quantitative framework for understanding historical landscape variability and evaluating the long-term consequences of forest disturbance and management.

title: West Nile Virus Forecasting
text:
West Nile virus (WNV) is the most common mosquito-borne disease in the United States, with more than 53,000 reported cases and 2,500 deaths since its introduction in 1999. The northern Great Plains have consistently experienced some of the highest WNV incidence rates in the country, with cases concentrated in particular geographic areas and outbreak years (Wimberly et al. 2013). Because WNV transmission is highly seasonal, weather conditions during spring and early summer influence virus amplification in mosquitoes and birds and the subsequent risk of human infection (Wimberly et al. 2014). Building on these findings, we developed regional forecasting models that initially used satellite observations of vegetation greenup and temperature-based degree days to predict WNV incidence (Chuang and Wimberly, 2012). Subsequent research demonstrated that integrating environmental indicators with mosquito infection surveillance improves forecasting accuracy, providing a stronger foundation for anticipating WNV outbreaks (Davis et al. 2017, 2018).
 ArboMAP forecasts of WNV in South Dakota, including historical calibration as well as predictions outside the range of the training data (Wimberly et al. 2022).
We translated these advances into the Arbovirus Monitoring and Prediction (ArboMAP) system, a set of tools for implementing WNV forecasting in public health agencies. ArboMAP has supported WNV forecasting in South Dakota since 2016, and was extended to Louisiana, Michigan, and Oklahoma (Nekorchuk et al. 2023). Retrospective validation demonstrated that models driven by environmental observations and mosquito surveillance data enabled accurate forecasts early enough to inform disease prevention and mosquito control before the peak transmission season (Wimberly et al. 2022). This work demonstrates the potential of integrating Earth observations and public health surveillance to move from reactive disease monitoring toward proactive outbreak preparedness. We are now developing ArboMAP 2.0, a next-generation forecasting platform that incorporates additional environmental data streams, improved modeling capabilities, and enhanced visualization tools to support broader implementation across multiple states.

title: Grassland Conservation
text:
North America’s grasslands are among its most threatened ecosystems, facing widespread conversion to agriculture and increasing encroachment by woody vegetation. These changes threaten biodiversity, fragment wildlife habitats, and diminish ecosystem services such as carbon storage, soil conservation, and water quality protection. Our research uses satellite Earth observations and geospatial analysis to quantify grassland loss, investigate its underlying drivers, and assess the ecological consequences of landscape transformation. We have focused particularly on the northern Great Plains, including the Prairie Pothole Region, where grasslands and wetlands provide critical habitat for migratory birds and other wildlife.
 Maps of the western corn belt showing conversion of grasslands to corn and soy agriculture (left) and conversion of corn and soy agriculture to grasslands (right) (Wright and Wimberly 2011).
Our studies have documented extensive grassland conversion associated with agricultural expansion in the western Corn Belt. Between 2007 and 2011, more than 500,000 hectares of grassland were converted to cropland, including substantial areas of previously undisturbed native prairie (Wright and Wimberly, 2013). We identified agricultural and socioeconomic factors associated with conversion, including farm size, land tenure, farm income, and crop productivity (Wimberly et al. 2017). We also demonstrated that remaining native grasslands in eastern South Dakota are highly fragmented, with connectivity among larger habitat areas dependent on networks of smaller, scattered patches (Wimberly et al. 2018). These findings highlight the importance of protecting remaining native prairie and maintaining landscape connectivity in regions undergoing agricultural intensification.
 Maps of the extent of Juniperus virginiana across eastern South Dakota derived from snow-covered Landsat imagery (Kaskie et al. 2019).
Woody plant encroachment represents a second major threat to Great Plains grasslands. The spread of eastern redcedar (Juniperus virginiana) alters grassland structure and habitat conditions, but early stages of invasion can be difficult to detect using conventional land cover maps. We developed satellite-based methods to quantify redcedar cover (Kaskie et al. 2019) and identify low-density stands where encroachment is beginning (Kaskie et al. 2022). These approaches provide tools for monitoring the spread of woody vegetation and identifying areas where early intervention may help prevent further grassland degradation.

title: Rural Health
text:
Geographic disparities in health reflect differences in the social, built, and natural environments where people live, as well as unequal access to health care and other essential resources. Our research has examined how these factors influence obesity, physical activity, and cancer care, with an emphasis on the distinctive challenges facing rural communities. Using county-level data from across the United States, we demonstrated that relationships between food environments and obesity differ between urban and rural settings. Obesity prevalence increased with distance to supermarkets in metropolitan counties, but no corresponding relationship was found in non-metropolitan counties (Michimi and Wimberly 2010a, Michimi and Wimberly 2010b). Additional research examined associations between obesity and the availability of different types of food retailers in major U.S. cities (Michimi and Wimberly 2015). In rural counties, greater availability of parks, trails, and other recreational amenities was associated with higher physical activity and lower obesity prevalence (Michimi and Wimberly 2012). Together, these findings highlight the importance of considering geographic context when evaluating environmental influences on health and developing strategies to promote healthier communities.
 Map of county-level obesity rates in the conterminous United States based on BRFSS data and smoothed using weighted head banging (Wimberly et al. 2010b).
We also investigated how rural isolation and geographic access to health care contribute to disparities in cancer diagnosis and treatment. In South Dakota, residents of isolated and economically disadvantaged rural communities were more likely to receive a late-stage colorectal cancer diagnosis (Lin and Wimberly 2017). We also found that breast cancer patients with better geographic access to radiation therapy facilities were more likely to receive radiation therapy rather than mastectomy (Lin et al. 2018). These studies demonstrate how geographic barriers to specialized health services may influence both the timing of cancer diagnosis and the treatment options available to rural populations, underscoring the importance of addressing spatial inequalities in health care access.

title: Tick-Borne Pathogens
text:
Ticks transmit a variety of disease-causing pathogens that are maintained in complex ecological cycles involving wildlife hosts and environmental conditions. The geographic distributions of ticks and their pathogens are influenced by climate, vegetation, and landscape characteristics, but these relationships vary across species and environmental settings. Our research has demonstrated that the environmental drivers of tick-borne pathogen distributions vary geographically, with climate playing a dominant role in the eastern United States and forest cover and fragmentation becoming more important near western range boundaries (Yabsley et al. 2005, Wimberly et al. 2008b). We also documented the effects of forest cover and flooding on pathogen distributions in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley (Manangan et al. 2007). Using Bayesian hierarchical models, we developed spatial predictions of tick-borne pathogen distributions that accounted for geographic variation in environmental relationships and spatial autocorrelation (Wimberly et al. 2008a). These studies demonstrated the importance of incorporating spatially heterogeneous environmental relationships into models of tick-borne disease risk.
 Map of the regional distribution of Ehrlichia chaffeensis based on a hierarchical Bayesian modeling incorporating spatially heterogeneous environmental predictors and spatial autocorrelation (Wimberly et al. 2008b).
More recently, we collaborated with Anni Yang (University of Oklahoma) to investigate how urban landscapes and microenvironments influence tick abundance. In a study of 13 parks in the Oklahoma City metropolitan area, we found that the abundance of lone star ticks (Amblyomma americanum) was influenced by both local habitat characteristics and broader landscape conditions (Marquez et al. 2025). Important predictors included woody vegetation, solar radiation, humidity, and soil characteristics at the local level and forest cover at the landscale scale. These findings highlight the highlight the potential for using environmental variables to predict potential areas of human exposure in urban green spaces.

title: EcoGRAPH
text:
The EcoGRAPH research group is based in the Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability at the University of Oklahoma. Our research investigates how changing climate and landscapes influence ecosystems and human health, integrating satellite Earth observations, environmental monitoring, and geospatial modeling to understand and anticipate these changes. We emphasize translating scientific knowledge into predictive tools and actionable information to support public health, land-use planning, and natural resource management.
Our work spans landscape to global scales, addressing topics such as climate-sensitive infectious diseases, forest degradation and wildfire, agricultural and urban expansion, and the ecological consequences of climate and land-use change. Through research collaborations across North America, Africa, and Asia, we seek to advance understanding of environmental change while developing practical approaches to anticipating and managing its impacts.

title: ArboMAP 2.0
text:
Arthropod-borne viruses such as West Nile virus (WNV) impose significant public health burdens across the United States. Although environmental drivers of transmission are well understood and forecasting techniques have advanced rapidly, operational uptake remains limited by fragmented tools, inconsistent workflows, and barriers to scalability. Building on more than a decade of development and real-world implementation, this project will create ArboMAP 2.0, a next-generation, nationally scalable platform for arbovirus risk forecasting and decision support. The goal is to transform ArboMAP from a successful regional forecasting system into a widely accessible, interoperable platform serving stakeholders at CDC and state and local health departments nationwide.
ArboMAP 2.0 will provide a unified, infrastructure for generating actionable forecasts of arbovirus risk across diverse ecological and institutional settings. The effort will combine technical modernization with coordinated stakeholder engagement to ensure the platform is scientifically robust, operationally relevant, and widely adopted. We will redesign the application with a modern, user-centered interface with simplified workflows, automated data ingestion, and clear visualization of risk and uncertainty to reduce barriers to adoption and support real-time decision-making. Modern software design frameworks will make it straightforward to deploy in the cloud, on local networks, or on individual workstations. Improved data integration with NASA Earth science datasets and public health surveillance will enable interoperability with a variety of public health data systems. The updated framework will support modular workflows that allow adaptation to multiple pathogens, locations, and data environments. Flexible model pipelines will accommodate new data types and emerging machine learning and AI modeling techniques.
A central component of this effort will be building a national community of ArboMAP users and contributors. We will develop connections with national and state health departments to co-develop use cases and pilot deployments. A user network will be established to share best practices in arbovirus forecasting and public health response. Training, documentation, and implementation toolkits will be tailored to the needs of public health practitioners. By lowering technical barriers and fostering a community of practice, the project will accelerate the translation of forecasting science into routine public health action. The resulting infrastructure will support earlier detection of outbreaks and better targeting vector control and disease prevention efforts. More broadly, this effort will provide a model for transforming forecasting models informed by NASA data into durable, national public health capabilities.

title: EPIDEMIA 2.0
text:
In Ethiopia, confirmed malaria cases have increased threefold since 2019. This resurgence is driven by multiple factors, including conflict, drug and insecticide resistance, and climate fluctuations. There is currently a strong demand for integrated surveillance and forecasting tools that can predict future outbreaks and allow proactive interventions to reduce outbreak severity. To address this needs, the Epidemic Prognosis Incorporating Disease and Environmental Monitoring for Integrated Assessment (EPIDEMIA) system was co-developed by a team us U.S. and Ethiopian scientists and public health professionals. EPIDEMIA is a suite of software tools uses forecasting models driven by NASA Earth Observations to predict epidemics associated with climate fluctuations. Advanced outbreak detection algorithms are also applied to predict epidemics driven by non-climatic factors. The system has been tested and piloted at a regional level, and the opportunities and barriers associated with broader implementation have been assessed. To support scale up, there is a need to enhance EPIDEMIA by expanding the utilization of NASA Earth observations, increasing forecasting accuracy, and improving the end user experience. The overarching goal of this project is to develop EPIDEMIA 2.0, a next-generation software system, by achieving the following objectives.

Improve the user interface to streamline the modeling process and support interactive visualization for decision support,
Integrate new sources of environmental data from satellite Earth observations,
Incorporate multiple modeling approaches for outbreak detection and forecasting, and
Include additional climate-sensitive diseases besides malaria.

This work builds upon previous work that included basic research to understand climate-malaria relationships, the development of software tools for predicting malaria, and engaging with public health stakeholders to understand the opportunities and barriers associated with national-level implementation of these tools. The research proposed here will substantially extend the previous work by supporting the sustainable expansion of EPIDEMIA throughout Ethiopia, incorporating additional streams of Earth observation data to enhance predictions, and extending the approach to other climate-sensitive diseases.

title: WAForDD
text:
The West Africa Forest Degradation Data system (WAForDD) was developed to provide annual estimates of canopy cover change in the forest reserves of Ghana. The system uses a historical Landsat imagery to generate a time series of canopy cover from 2001-present, along with disturbance and recovery rates from 2003-present. Canopy cover is estimated using a random forests machine learning algorithm and extensive training and validation datasets derived from very-high resolution satellite imagery. The LandTrendr temporal segmentation is then applied to the canopy cover time series for each pixel to distinguish forest disturbance and recovery from periods of relative stability. We found that this approach can detect forest degradation that results in partial canopy removal as well as complete forest loss and post-disturbance recovery. Canopy cover remained relatively stable in protected areas such as National Parks, but was reduced by forest degradation and loss from logging, fire, illegal mining, and agricultural encroachment in many of the other forest reserves.
 Closed canopy forest in the Bobiri Reserve, Ghana.
WAForDD is implemented using Google Earth Engine (GEE), a cloud-based platform for geospatial analysis that provides access to the Landsat archive as well as many other Earth observation datasets. GEE has enabled the transfer of WAForDD to partners organization in Ghana by providing access to data and code through a cloud-based integrated development environment. This approach eliminates the need to download, store, and process large volumes of remote sensing imagery on local systems. We also developed a stand-alone Earth Engine App to facilitate data visualization and summarization. GEE programmers can explore the code archive and read the project documentation for more detailed information. Those wishing to explore the annual change data in more detail should use the WaforDD App.
We have collaborated with our partners to continue updating WAForDD anually. The remote sensing methods and validation of the forest degradation dataset are documented in a peer-reviewed journal article (Wimberly et al. 2022). The WAForDD dataset has been applied in several research projects, including a study of the drivers of fire and non-fire disturbances (Wanyama et al. 2023), and an analysis of post-disturbance forest recovery rates that combined WAForDD data with forest biomass and structure data from the GEDI mission (Wanyama et al. 2025).
 Forest change maps from the West Africa Forest Degradation Data system (WAForDD) Version 2.1. The maps show the Desiri, Tano Offin, and Tano Offin Extension reserves.
